triples.rationale: The opening verse introduces the Lord's word to Jonah. Chapter 3 explicitly says that the word came to him a second time, marking the renewal of this commission after his flight and rescue.
triples.source_text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, the son of Amittai, saying:

target_units.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:

triples.rationale: The Lord sends Jonah against Nineveh because its wickedness has come up before Him. Genesis similarly presents Sodom and Gomorrah's increasing cry and great sins as coming before the Lord ahead of intervention concerning the cities.
triples.source_text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it, for the outcry of its wickedness has come up to Me.”

target_units.text: And the Lord said, “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has increased, and their sins are exceedingly great.
So I will go down and see whether they are being brought to an end according to their cry which comes to Me; and if not, that I may know.”

triples.relationship: flight from God's presence and the sea
triples.rationale: Jonah boards a ship in an attempt to flee from the Lord's presence. The psalm asks where anyone could flee from God's face and says that even at the sea's farthest reaches His hand remains present.
triples.source_text: But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa, found a ship traveling to Tarshish, paid its fare and boarded it, to sail with them to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.

target_units.text: Where can I go from Thy Spirit, and where can I flee from Thy face?
If I ascend to heaven, Thou art there; if I descend into Hades, Thou art present.
if I take up my wings at dawn and settle at the sea’s farthest reaches,
indeed, even there Thy hand will guide me, and Thy right hand will hold me fast.

triples.relationship: the Lord raises a storm at sea
triples.rationale: Jonah's ship is endangered when the Lord raises a great wind and sea surge. The psalm's account of seafarers likewise attributes a storm wind and rising waves to the Lord's command.
triples.source_text: The Lord stirred up a wind upon the sea, and there was a great surge on the sea; the ship was in danger of being shattered.

target_units.text: Those going down into the sea in ships, doing work on many waters,
they saw the Lord’s works and His wonders in the depth.
He spoke, and a storm wind stood, and its waves were raised.

triples.relationship: narrative parallel of a sleeper in a storm
triples.rationale: Jonah sleeps below while the sailors fear for their storm-tossed ship. Mark likewise places a sleeping central figure in a boat endangered by a great storm. The comparison concerns the narrative situation; Jonah's flight and Jesus' later command have different roles in their respective stories.
triples.source_text: The sailors were afraid, and each was crying out to their god. They threw the equipment in the ship into the sea, to lighten their load. But Jonah had gone down into the hollow of the ship, and was sleeping and snoring.

target_units.text: A great windstorm arose, and the waves broke into the boat, so that the boat was already filling.
He was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke Him and said to Him, “Teacher, dost Thou not care that we are perishing?”

triples.rationale: Jonah's sailors throw equipment into the sea to lighten the ship during the storm. Acts describes storm-battered sailors throwing cargo and then the ship's tackle overboard.
triples.source_text: The sailors were afraid, and each was crying out to their god. They threw the equipment in the ship into the sea, to lighten their load. But Jonah had gone down into the hollow of the ship, and was sleeping and snoring.

target_units.text: As we were violently battered by the storm, the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands.

triples.relationship: narrative parallel of awakening the sleeper
triples.rationale: The officer calls Jonah to rise from sleep and pray so that those aboard will not perish. Mark's disciples likewise awaken Jesus with a question about their perishing, connecting the awakening with the boat's danger.
triples.source_text: The ship’s officer approached him and said, “Why are you snoring? Rise and call upon your god, so that the god may bring us safely through and we may not perish.”

target_units.text: He was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke Him and said to Him, “Teacher, dost Thou not care that we are perishing?”

triples.rationale: The sailors use lots and Jonah is identified as the cause of their trouble. Joshua narrates the successive indication of Judah, a clan and finally Achar in the investigation of Israel's offense. The shared pattern is identification of a particular offender within a larger afflicted group; Joshua's supplied wording says indicated.
triples.source_text: Each said to his neighbor, “Come, let us cast lots and learn on whose account this calamity is among us.” They cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.

target_units.text: Joshua rose early and brought the people forward by tribes. The tribe of Judah was indicated.
They were brought forward by clans, and the Zerahite clan was indicated. They were brought forward man by man,
and Achar son of Zambri, son of Zerah, was indicated.

triples.rationale: After Jonah is identified, the sailors demand an account of the cause of their calamity and his background. Joshua similarly questions the identified Achar, demanding disclosure of what he has done, and receives a confession.
triples.source_text: They said to him, “Tell us on whose account this calamity is among us. What is your occupation? Where do you come from? What country and what people are you from?”

target_units.text: Joshua said to Achar, “Give glory today to the Lord, the God of Israel, and make confession. Tell me what you have done, and do not hide it from me.”
Achar answered Joshua, “Truly I have sinned before the Lord, the God of Israel. This is what I did:

triples.relationship: shared confession of the Lord as creator
triples.rationale: Jonah identifies the God he reveres as the Lord of heaven who made the sea and dry land. Exodus likewise describes the Lord as maker of heaven, earth and sea, explaining the scope of the deity Jonah names while at sea.
triples.source_text: He said to them, “I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

target_units.text: For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.

triples.relationship: same-chapter progression of the sailors' fear
triples.rationale: The sailors first fear greatly on learning of Jonah's flight from the Lord. After the sea is calmed, verse 16 again describes their great fear, now explicitly directed to the Lord and expressed in sacrifice and vows.
triples.source_text: The men were greatly afraid and said to him, “What is this you have done?” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

target_units.text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

triples.relationship: same-chapter proposed remedy and narrated outcome
triples.rationale: Jonah says that throwing him into the sea will make it cease raging against the sailors. Verse 15 narrates that action and the sea's resulting cessation, completing the proposal with its stated outcome.
triples.source_text: Jonah said to them, “Lift me up and throw me into the sea; then the sea will subside for you. For I know that this great surge is upon you because of me.”

target_units.text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

triples.relationship: parallel unsuccessful rowing against hostile conditions
triples.rationale: The men strain to return Jonah's ship to land but cannot overcome the sea. Mark describes disciples straining at the rowing because the wind is against them, a corresponding scene of difficult human effort on hostile waters.
triples.source_text: But the men strained to return to land and could not, for the sea kept rising more fiercely against them.

target_units.text: When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and He was alone on the land.
Seeing them straining at the rowing, for the wind was against them, He came toward them about the fourth watch of the night, walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them.

triples.rationale: The sailors ask the Lord not to lay innocent blood upon them as they prepare to throw Jonah overboard. Deuteronomy provides a communal plea that innocent-blood guilt not remain among the people; both prayers explicitly seek release from that bloodguilt.
triples.source_text: They cried out to the Lord and said, “By no means, Lord! May we not perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for Thou, Lord, hast done as Thou didst wish.”

target_units.text: Be merciful unto Thy people Israel, whom Thou hast redeemed, O Lord, out of the land of Egypt, that there be no guilt of innocent blood among Thy people Israel. And atonement shall be made for the blood on their behalf.
And you shall remove the guilt of innocent blood from among yourselves, if you do that which is good and pleasing before the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: prayer followed by the storm's cessation
triples.rationale: The sea ceases after the sailors' prayer and their action toward Jonah. The psalm likewise narrates seafarers crying to the Lord and the storm being commanded to settle, with the waves falling silent.
triples.source_text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

target_units.text: They cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and He brought them out of their distresses,
and commanded the storm, and it settled into a breeze, and its waves fell silent.

triples.rationale: Jonah's narrative moves from a raging sea to its cessation when he is thrown overboard. Mark narrates wind ceasing and a great calm after Jesus' command; both episodes emphasize the abrupt end of a dangerous storm, while specifying different actions preceding it.
triples.source_text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

target_units.text: And He awoke, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Be silent; be still.” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

triples.relationship: sacrifice and vows in response to deliverance
triples.rationale: The sailors offer sacrifice and vows to the Lord after the sea calms. The psalmist likewise promises burnt offerings and payment of vows declared in affliction, joining distress, deliverance and worship.
triples.source_text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

target_units.text: I will enter Thy house with whole burnt offerings; I will pay Thee my vows,
which my lips declared and my mouth spoke in my affliction.

triples.relationship: fear following the calming of the sea
triples.rationale: Jonah's sailors greatly fear the Lord after the storm ends. Mark's disciples are greatly afraid after Jesus calms the wind and sea and ask who He is, connecting the resulting fear with power over the waters.
triples.source_text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

target_units.text: They were greatly afraid and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”
